title: Why Do We Hear Thunder After Lightning, According to Science Today?
parts: A flash lights up the sky over the water. Now count. One second. Five. Ten.
Only then does the thunder arrive.
So why do we hear thunder after we see lightning?
First, where does thunder come from? The National Weather Service says it is created when lightning passes through the air.
The discharge heats the air rapidly, and the air expands.
Environment Canada calls thunder the sound of the shockwave that lightning produces.
An American atmospheric research center says thunder and lightning happen at roughly the same time. So it is a race, and it is not close.
Environment Canada says light travels three hundred thousand kilometers per second, and sound about three tenths of a kilometer per second.
Our arithmetic: light is about a million times faster, so you see the flash almost at once.
The National Weather Service puts it plainly. Thunder takes about five seconds to travel a mile.
Our comparison: the delay is a tape measure. Count the seconds from flash to thunder.
The National Weather Service says divide by five to get miles.
Environment Canada says divide by three to get kilometers.
Our arithmetic: ten seconds is about two miles, or about three kilometers.
Environment Canada adds that sound moves faster in hot air and slower in cold air. Our reading: treat the count as an estimate.
But thunder is not always one bang. Often it rumbles.
Environment Canada says sound from each part of the strike reaches you at a different time.
When the lightning channel runs across your line of sight, it says, you hear a clap.
When it runs roughly along your line of sight, you hear a rumble.
Wikipedia says rumbles can last for more than thirty seconds.
Our reading: a long bolt does not make one sound. It makes a stretch of sound, spread out in time.
How far can you hear it? The National Weather Service says thunder can be heard only about ten miles from the strike.
The American research center also says so-called heat lightning is cloud-to-cloud lightning seen from beyond the horizon. Its thunder is too far away to hear.
The National Weather Service also says lightning often strikes more than three miles from the center of a thunderstorm.
Its rule: when thunder roars, go indoors, and stay there until thirty minutes after the last thunder you hear.
Our reading: the delay is not a flaw. It is a warning with a ruler built in.
So next storm, from indoors, count the seconds.
Not every clue hides in the sky. Some sit on your desk.
Fold an A4 sheet of paper in half. The shape stays the same. Why?
